claims.text: McDonnell Douglas's interest was corporate self-protection - a prime contractor conducting proprietary research into an aerospace capability it did not possess. Reasoning: this matches the incentive structure later codified in DoD IR&D policy and named by Grusch, but no McDonnell Douglas internal record of the study has been released.

conflicts: Wood is the principal proponent of the authenticity of the Majestic-12 documents, a contested body of material; his corporate testimony and his documents work should be graded separately.

label: Robert M. Wood
narrative: Wood is the documented instance of a prime contractor spending its own money to study the phenomenon - the IR&D pattern in its earliest and most benign form. A Cornell physics PhD, he spent his career at McDonnell Douglas Astronautics in Southern California on missile and space systems, and in the late 1960s ran a company-funded study of unidentified craft out of the Huntington Beach facility, on the reasoning that if the propulsion were real the company needed to know about it before a competitor did. That study is the direct ancestor of every later corporate 'internal interest' in the subject: not a government contract, not congressionally visible, funded from within the firm. After retiring in 1993 Wood turned to the documentary record, building with his son Ryan the majesticdocuments.com archive and applying forensic tests - typography, paper, security markings, terminology dating - to the Majestic-12 and related papers. That work is contested and the board treats the documents themselves as unresolved. Wood's value here is structural rather than evidentiary: he is a named senior engineer at a prime contractor who confirms from the inside that the primes looked, that they looked on their own dime, and that what they found was not reported anywhere Congress could see it.
